---
title: "Real Numbers"
---

::: {.claim}
**Claim.** There exists a unique positive $r \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t. $r^2 = 2$. Denote $r$ by $\sqrt{2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Take the set $A := \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 2\}$.
We first show that $\sup A$ exists.

1. $A$ is bounded above: $\forall x \in A$, $x^2 < 2$. Then, $x^2 < 4$.
   We know that $x \geq 2 \Rightarrow x^2 \geq 4$, so taking the contrapositive gives us $x < 2$. Thus, $2$ is an upper bound of $A$.
2. $A$ is nonempty: $1 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $1^2 = 1 < 2$. Then $1 \in A$.

Let $r := \sup A$. We then show that $r^2 = 2$.

1. ($r^2 \geq 2$):

   Take a positive number $s$ s.t. $s^2 < 2$. We wish to find an $h > 0$ s.t. $(s+h)^2 < 2$. Since $2 - s^2 > 0$, $\dfrac{2 - s^2}{2s+1} > 0$.
   We choose $h$ s.t. $0 < h < \dfrac{2-s^2}{2s+1}$, and also that $h < 1$.
   Note that
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   (s+h)^2 - s^2 &= 2sh + h^2 \\
   &= h(2s+h) \\
   &< h(2s+1) && [h < 1] \\
   &< 2 - s^2 && \left[h < \tfrac{2-s^2}{2s+1}\right]
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   and thus $(s+h)^2 < 2$, so $s + h \in A$.
   Since we found an $h > 0$ s.t. $s+h \in A$, $s < s+h \leq \sup A = r$.
   Thus $s < r \ \forall s \in A$.
   Suppose $r^2 < 2$. Then $r \in A$, and so from the argument above, $r < r$.
   This is a contradiction. Thus, $r^2 \geq 2$.

2. ($r^2 \leq 2$):

   Take a positive number $s$ s.t. $s^2 > 2$. If we show that $r < s$ for any $s$, then $r^2 \leq 2$.

   To show the inequality, we show that for an $h > 0$, $s - h$ is an upper bound for $A$, and thus $r \leq s - h < s$. We need $(s-h)^2 > 2$ and $s - h > 0$. Since $s^2 - 2 > 0$, $\dfrac{s^2-2}{2s} > 0$. We let $h = \dfrac{s^2-2}{2s}$.

   I: $\displaystyle s - h = s - \frac{s^2-2}{2s} = \frac{s}{2} + \frac{1}{s} > 0$

   II:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   s^2 - (s-h)^2 &= 2sh - h^2 \\
   &< 2sh \\
   &= s^2 - 2 && \left[h = \tfrac{s^2-2}{2s}\right]
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   Thus, $(s-h)^2 > 2$.
   If $x \geq s - h$, then $x^2 \geq (s-h)^2 > 2$, so $x \notin A$. Thus, $s - h$ is an upper bound of $A$.

3. Since we showed both inequalities, $r^2 = 2$.

Finally, we show Uniqueness. Suppose $s \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t. $s^2 = 2$ and $s > 0$.
Then, $s^2 = r^2$. However, if $s < r$ then $s^2 < r^2$, and if $r < s$ then $r^2 < s^2$. Thus, $s = r$. [$\square$]{style="float: right;"}
:::

::: {#thm-archimedean name="Archimedean Property"}
If $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x > 0$, then there exists an $n \in \mathbb{N}$ s.t. $nx > y$.
:::

::: {.proof}
This is equivalent to stating that for every real number $t := \frac{y}{x}$, $\exists\, n \in \mathbb{N}$ s.t. $n > t$. This is equivalently stating that $\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is not bounded above.

Suppose for contradiction that $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above. Let $b = \sup \mathbb{N}$. $b - 1$ cannot be an upper bound for $\mathbb{N}$. Then, $\exists\, m \in \mathbb{N}$ s.t. $m > b - 1$. Then, $m + 1 > b$. But $m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}$, so $b$ is not an upper bound for $\mathbb{N}$.

[We utilize the LUB property of $\mathbb{R}$ for the existence of $\sup \mathbb{N}$.]
:::

::: {#thm-density-of-q name="Density of $\mathbb{Q}$"}
If $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x < y$, then there exists a $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ s.t. $x < q < y$.
:::

::: {.proof}
```{=html}
<div style="position: relative; max-width: 380px; height: 92px; margin: 0.5rem auto 1.25rem;">
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 46px; left: 0; right: 0; border-top: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 39px; left: 16%; height: 14px; border-left: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 39px; left: 30%; height: 14px; border-left: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 39px; left: 48%; height: 14px; border-left: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 39px; left: 64%; height: 14px; border-left: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <div style="position: absolute; top: 39px; left: 82%; height: 14px; border-left: 1.5px solid currentColor;"></div>
  <span style="position: absolute; bottom: 52px; left: 16%; transform: translateX(-50%);">\(\frac{m-1}{n}\)</span>
  <span style="position: absolute; bottom: 52px; left: 48%; transform: translateX(-50%);">\(\frac{m}{n}\)</span>
  <span style="position: absolute; bottom: 52px; left: 82%; transform: translateX(-50%);">\(\frac{m+1}{n}\)</span>
  <span style="position: absolute; top: 56px; left: 30%; transform: translateX(-50%);">\(x\)</span>
  <span style="position: absolute; top: 56px; left: 64%; transform: translateX(-50%);">\(y\)</span>
</div>
```

Assume that $x \geq 0$. Note that $y - x > 0$. By the [Archimedean property](#thm-archimedean){.quarto-xref}, $\exists\, n \in \mathbb{N}$ s.t. $y - x > \frac{1}{n}$.

Define $A = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\}$. By [AP](#thm-archimedean){.quarto-xref}, $A$ is non-empty. By WOP, $A$ has a least element $m$.
$m > nx \Rightarrow x < \frac{m}{n}$.
$m - 1 \notin A$, so $m - 1 \leq nx \Rightarrow m \leq nx + 1$.

On the other hand, from $n(y-x) > 1$ we have $ny > 1 + nx$.
Thus, $ny > m \Rightarrow y > \frac{m}{n}$. We take $q = \frac{m}{n}$.

For $x < 0$, if $y > 0$ then $q = 0$. If $y \leq 0$, then we find $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ s.t. $-y < r < -x$ and let $q = -r$. [$\square$]{style="float: right;"}
:::

**Triangle Inequality**: $|x + y| \leq |x| + |y|$

**Reverse Triangle Inequality**: $\big||x| - |y|\big| \leq |x - y|$

::: {.proof}
$|x| = |x - y + y| \leq |x - y| + |y|$
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\Rightarrow |x| - |y| \leq |x - y| \quad \text{(i)}. \text{ Similarly,} \\
&\phantom{\Rightarrow{}} |y| - |x| \leq |x - y| \\
&\Rightarrow -(|x| - |y|) \leq |x - y| \\
&\Rightarrow |x| - |y| \geq -|x - y| \quad \text{(ii)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus, $-|x - y| \leq |x| - |y| \leq |x - y|$
$$
\Rightarrow \big||x| - |y|\big| \leq |x - y|
$$
[$\square$]{style="display: block; text-align: right;"}
:::

::: {#thm-cantor-reals name="Cantor"}
$\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
:::
